sn35.92:2.2: The same “duality” is described as the (sentient) body and “external” name and form, which are essential for contact through the six senses ([sn12.19:1.3]()). This recalls the ‘duality” spoken of by Yājñavalkya as his culminating philosophy: “For when there is a duality, as it were, then one can smell the other, one can see them other, one can hear the other, one can taste the other, one can speak to the other, one can think of the other, one can cognize the other. By what would one cognize that which cognizes all this? By what would one cognize the cognizer?” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14)It is not obvious how the “duality” of existence and nonexistence can be reconciled with the claim here ([sn22.90:9.2]()).
